name: Tummo breathing

image.caption: Tanumanasi Los seis yogas de Naropa Tumo Tummo

lead: Tummo, or inner fire, is a practice from Tibetan Vajrayana Buddhism that combines breath control, visualisation and meditation to raise body heat. Its main purpose is spiritual. Some people in wellness and biohacking circles also use tummo-style breathing in routines with cold exposure.

People who adopt it hope for better stress control, steadier energy and the lifestyle benefits that come with a consistent breathing and cold routine. Lab studies of monks and trained Westerners found rises in body temperature, and the closely related Wim Hof Method has a small research literature with mixed results.

paras: Traditional tummo is taught within a lineage, with a teacher and preparatory practices. In wellness settings it appears as a breathing session, often in the morning with light exposure and cold exposure, in routines posted by T Nation forum users.

Forceful breathing can cause lightheadedness and brief loss of consciousness, and the related Wim Hof breathing has been linked to drownings when done in water. Heart and cold-exposure precautions are advised by heart associations.

angle.text: Tummo-style breathing is used by some as part of a morning cold and light routine, for warmth and calm. Any appearance effect would come indirectly through stress, sleep and training consistency.

lead: Tummo (Tibetan gtum mo, Sanskrit candali), meaning 'fierce woman' or 'inner fire', is a tantric practice of Tibetan Vajrayana Buddhism. It uses vase breathing, in which the breath is held low in the abdomen, with visualisation of a flame at the navel to produce heat [1][2]. It is part of the Six Dharmas of Naropa and is taught as a completion-stage practice [1].

The tradition's goal is spiritual. In looks and fitness circles it is mentioned as a breathing method to pair with cold exposure and morning routines, in the same family as the Wim Hof Method [3]. People hope for a calmer mood, better stress regulation and a warmer body during cold exposure, which can support consistent training and general wellbeing.

Scientists have measured it: a 1982 Nature report found finger and toe temperatures rose by roughly 3 to 8 degrees C in monks during practice [1][4], and a 2013 study found large core temperature rises in expert meditators and that Westerners could raise temperature using breathing alone [5].

paras: Practitioners visualise the body's channels, winds and drops, hold the breath low in the abdomen in vase breathing and imagine a fiery syllable at the navel; the heat is said to draw winds into the central channel and produce bliss [1]. Traditions differ in detail [1].

The practice appears in Indian tantric texts such as the Hevajra Tantra and in the Six Dharmas of Naropa, and reached Tibet in the 11th century through Marpa and then Milarepa [1][2]. Western interest grew after temperature studies in the 1980s [4].

A 2013 PLOS ONE study measured axillary temperature and EEG in expert meditators in eastern Tibet and compared them with Western non-meditators trained in vase breathing alone [5]. A 2024 systematic review of the Wim Hof Method, a related breathing and cold regimen, reported small studies with mixed outcomes [6], and a case study of Wim Hof and his twin examined brown fat and cold-induced thermogenesis [7]. A 2025 report examined brain activity during tummo meditation and Niguma yoga [8].

Studies are small physiological experiments rather than treatment trials. They include temperature measurements in monks [4], the 2013 meditator and control study [5], and the Wim Hof systematic review [6][7][8].

The Wim Hof breathing exercises can cause hyperventilation and brief unconsciousness, and deaths by drowning have been reported when done in water; heart associations advise consulting a physician before cold exposure [9].
